questions.question: In most libraries and standards, which names refer to the same curve as NIST P-256?
options: P-256, secp256r1, and prime256v1
P-256 and secp256k1
P-256 and Curve25519
P-256 and Ed25519
questions.explanation: NIST P-256 is also commonly called secp256r1 and prime256v1 in different ecosystems.

questions.question: What is the defining short-Weierstrass curve equation form for P-256 over its prime field?
options: y² ≡ x³ − 3x + b (mod p)
y² ≡ x³ + 7 (mod p)
B·y² ≡ x³ + A·x² + x (mod p)
y² ≡ x³ + ax² + b (mod 2)
questions.explanation: P-256 uses a = −3 (mod p) in short-Weierstrass form: y² = x³ + a·x + b.

questions.question: What does a “rigid” curve generation procedure aim to minimize?
options: The discretionary freedom to choose constants, reducing room for hidden trapdoor selection
The need for point validation during parsing
The existence of modular square roots in the field
The size of the curve order n to make operations faster
questions.explanation: Rigidity is about reducing degrees of freedom in parameter choice so constants look like “nothing up my sleeve” outputs.

questions.question: In a compressed SEC1 P-256 public key, what information does the first byte (0x02 or 0x03) encode?
options: Whether the y-coordinate is even or odd
Whether the x-coordinate is even or odd
Whether the point has prime order
Whether the scalar was clamped
questions.explanation: Compressed encodings keep x and one bit of y parity to choose between y and −y (mod p).

questions.question: For primes p ≡ 3 (mod 4), what is a standard way to compute sqrt(a) (mod p) when it exists?
options: Compute a^((p+1)/4) (mod p) and verify the result squares to a
Compute a^(p−1) (mod p) and use it directly as the root
Compute a^((p−1)/2) (mod p) and treat it as the root
Square a repeatedly until it becomes a
questions.explanation: When p ≡ 3 (mod 4), exponentiation to (p+1)/4 yields a square root for quadratic residues, and you still verify.

questions.question: Attack scenario: in ECDH, what is the core check that prevents invalid-curve / invalid-point attacks?
options: Verify the peer point is correctly encoded and lies on the intended curve before any secret scalar multiplication
Verify the peer x-coordinate is less than the group order n
Verify the peer key uses compressed encoding (not uncompressed)
Verify the peer y-coordinate is odd
questions.explanation: The essential defense is validating the input point: encoding rules and on-curve checks must happen before multiplying by a secret.

questions.question: When parsing an uncompressed public key (04 || x || y), why should an implementation reject x or y values ≥ p?
options: To enforce canonical field element encoding and avoid ambiguous representations
Because x and y must always be less than n (the group order)
Because x and y are defined to be little-endian values
Because P-256 forbids even x-coordinates
questions.explanation: Field elements are taken modulo p, but encodings should be canonical: coordinates must be in the range 0..p−1.

questions.question: What is the standard validity range for a P-256 private key scalar k, assuming the group order is n?
options: 1 ≤ k < n
0 ≤ k ≤ n
1 ≤ k ≤ p
0 ≤ k < p
questions.explanation: Private scalars are reduced modulo n, but 0 is rejected; the conventional range is 1..n−1.
